summary: Chlorthalidone is a long-acting thiazide-like diuretic (action 48-72 hours) used to treat hypertension, alone or with other agents, and as adjunctive therapy for edema in heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, corticosteroid/estrogen therapy, and renal dysfunction. It increases urinary excretion of sodium and chloride at the cortical diluting segment. A single morning dose with food is recommended. Monitor for hypokalemia, hyperuricemia, and hyperglycemia.
indications: Hypertension (sole agent or to enhance other antihypertensives)
Edema associated with congestive heart failure
Edema associated with hepatic cirrhosis and with corticosteroid/estrogen therapy
Edema due to renal dysfunction (nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis, chronic renal failure)

dosage.n: Doses above 100 mg/day usually add no benefit; K loss is dose-related

admin: Initiate at the lowest possible dose and titrate to response
Give a single dose in the morning with food
Monitor and replace potassium as needed
Caution when combining with other antihypertensives (additive/potentiated effect)
moa: Chlorthalidone is a thiazide-like (monosulfamyl) diuretic that acts primarily at the cortical diluting segment of the distal nephron to inhibit sodium and chloride reabsorption, producing copious diuresis with increased sodium and chloride excretion. The major portion is excreted unchanged by the kidneys. Its antihypertensive action involves an initial fall in plasma volume and cardiac output and, with chronic use, reduced peripheral vascular resistance.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to chlorthalidone or other sulfonamide-derived drugs
relative: Impaired hepatic function / progressive liver disease (electrolyte shifts may precipitate hepatic coma)
History of allergy or bronchial asthma

preg: Routine diuretic use in an otherwise healthy pregnant woman is inappropriate. Diuretics do not prevent or treat toxemia. Use only when edema is due to pathologic causes. Thiazides cross the placenta; risks include fetal/neonatal jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and other adult-type reactions. (Legacy Category B by animal data.)
lact: Thiazides are excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the nursing infant, decide whether to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering its importance to the mother.
renal: Use with caution in severe renal disease; may precipitate azotemia, and cumulative effects may develop in renal impairment. Thiazide-like diuretics lose efficacy at low GFR.
hepatic: Use with caution in impaired hepatic function or progressive liver disease; minor fluid/electrolyte changes may precipitate hepatic coma.

major: Lithium — reduced renal clearance increases lithium toxicity risk
Other antihypertensives / ganglionic and peripheral adrenergic blockers — potentiated hypotension
moderate: Digitalis glycosides — hypokalemia increases digitalis toxicity risk
Insulin / oral hypoglycemics — altered glucose control; may need dose change
minor: May decrease arterial responsiveness to norepinephrine (not clinically limiting)
interactions.food: Take with food in the morning; food does not impair efficacy.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol, barbiturates, or narcotics may aggravate orthostatic hypotension.
interactions.diagnostics: May raise serum uric acid, glucose, and calcium and lower serum potassium and sodium.

monitoring: Serum potassium, sodium, and chloride periodically
Serum uric acid and blood glucose
Blood pressure and signs of volume depletion
Signs of potassium loss (weakness, cramps, palpitations)
counsel: Take in the morning to avoid night-time urination
Report excessive thirst, tiredness, drowsiness, muscle cramps, nausea, vomiting, or rapid heartbeat (possible low potassium)
Rise slowly from sitting/lying to reduce dizziness
Limit alcohol, which can increase dizziness
Tell your doctor if you have diabetes, gout, lupus, kidney or liver disease
Inform your doctor of all medicines, especially lithium and digoxin
pk: Diuretic effect over the dosing day
pearls: Longer-acting and, mg-for-mg, more potent for blood pressure than hydrochlorothiazide; favored for once-daily 24-hour antihypertensive control
Electrolyte effects (low K, low Na) and metabolic effects (high uric acid, high glucose, high calcium) are dose-related — use the lowest effective dose
Single morning dose with food is recommended; divided dosing is unnecessary
Watch potassium closely when co-prescribed with digoxin (hypokalemia potentiates toxicity)
Loses diuretic efficacy at low GFR; avoid/caution in severe renal disease
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is late in the day or close to the next dose, skip it (to avoid night-time diuresis). Do not double the dose.
overdose: Symptoms include nausea, weakness, dizziness, and electrolyte disturbances. There is no specific antidote; gastric lavage may be used, followed by supportive treatment including, where necessary, cautious IV dextrose-saline with potassium and correction of fluid/electrolyte imbalance.
